Are you a product team or a feature team? Are you building the right things to achieve your company’s vision, or are you simply delivering features because they have been requested? These questions point to an important aspect of Product Management: having a product vision is not enough. You need a strategy to turn that vision into reality. What is product strategy? Simply put, a strategy is a deliberate approach to achieving a goal, particularly when the path to that goal is uncertain. Product strategy applies this thinking to a product. It defines the choices a company makes about its target customers, the problems it intends to solve, the value it aims to deliver, and the approach it will take to achieve its business objectives. It helps answer three important questions: Where do we want to go? What opportunities will help us get there? What will we prioritize to make progress? Without a clear strategy, product teams risk spending time and resources building features that may not meaningfully contribute to the product vision or business goals. Four elements of product strategy In his writing on product strategy, Marty Cagan of Silicon Valley Product Group (SVPG) highlights four key elements: focus, insights, actions, and management. 1. Focus: Decide what matters most Not everything a company does will have the same impact. Product strategy requires making deliberate choices about which objectives deserve attention and which initiatives can best move the business forward. This means being willing to say no to good ideas that are not the right priorities at the moment. For example, an education product might have several potential improvements: introducing new courses, redesigning its dashboard, adding gamification, or improving course completion rates. The team must determine which opportunity is most important to its users and business goals rather than attempting to pursue everything at once. The lesson: Strategy requires choices. Focus on the few things that can make the greatest difference. 2. Insights: Understand where the opportunities are Once the team has identified what matters, it needs insights to determine how to make progress. These insights come from studying the business, analyzing data, learning from customers, examining competitors, understanding market dynamics, and evaluating emerging technologies and internal capabilities. The goal is not simply to collect information. It is to develop an understanding that can inform better product decisions. For example, a team might assume that users are abandoning a course because the content is too difficult. However, user interviews and product analytics could reveal that learners are struggling to find time to complete lessons. These two explanations would lead to different product decisions. This is why product managers must go beyond assumptions and invest in research, critical thinking, and analysis. The lesson: Better product decisions begin with a better understanding of the problem and the opportunities available. 3. Actions: Turn insights into decisions Insights alone do not create value. They become useful when translated into deliberate actions. Once a team understands what matters and identifies promising opportunities, it must decide what to do about them. This involves selecting initiatives, defining priorities, allocating resources, and making trade-offs. Returning to the education product example, if research reveals that users struggle to find time for lessons, the team might test shorter lessons or introduce progress reminders before investing in an entirely new course catalogue. The important point is that the action should follow from the insight and contribute to the intended outcome. A product roadmap can communicate these priorities, but a list of features is not a strategy. The strategy explains why those initiatives matter and how they are expected to advance the product vision. The lesson: Connect every major initiative to an insight, a strategic choice, and a desired outcome. 4. Management: Keep the team moving in the right direction Even a well-defined strategy can fail if it is not effectively communicated, understood, and managed. Product leaders must help teams understand the direction, align stakeholders, monitor progress, and adapt when new evidence emerges. This does not mean controlling every task. It means creating the conditions for teams to make good decisions while ensuring their work remains aligned with the strategy. For example, a team might discover during development that a planned feature is more complex than expected. The product manager must help assess the implications, revisit priorities where necessary, and ensure the team remains focused on the intended outcome.
